title: Comparative Study of Quantum-Circuit Scalability in a Financial Problem
abstract_summary: This preprint analyzes the scaling of quantum circuits required for quantum amplitude estimation applied to a simplified T-Bill pricing problem, comparing superconducting (IBM) and ion-trap (IonQ) hardware. By counting two-qubit gates after transpilation for 1–19 evaluation qubits, the authors show that ion-trap systems require roughly two to three times fewer two-qubit gates due to all-to-all connectivity and native entangling gates, whereas superconducting devices incur extra SWAPs and higher gate counts driven by limited topology.
methodology_description: The study conducts a comparative, device-aware analysis of quantum-circuit scalability for a simplified financial pricing problem (single-step T-Bill modeled as a binomial with outcomes mapped to |0> and |1>). The authors construct Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) circuits that encode a probability p via a single-objective rotation A = RY(θ) with θ = 2 arcsin(√p), and vary the number of evaluation qubits n (accuracy/resolution parameter). For each n they (1) build/optimize the QAE circuit (Hadamards on evaluation qubits, controlled Q/CRY gates for amplitude amplification, and inverse QFT), (2) decompose CRY and CX into native gates appropriate to each hardware family (IBM superconducting basis gates: CX, RZ, SX, etc.; IonQ ion-trap basis: single-qubit rotations and Mølmer–Sørensen (MS)/RXX two-qubit interactions), (3) transpile the circuits to target backends/topologies using Qiskit (including handling SWAP insertion due to limited connectivity), (4) count two-qubit gates after transpilation for different backends (ideal all-to-all IBM model, IBM Yorktown, IBM Tokyo, IBM Cairo, and IonQ), and (5) repeat placement/transpilation runs for real IBM topologies to capture variability from routing and then fit polynomial models to the observed two-qubit gate counts versus n to quantify scaling differences. The primary metric is the post-transpilation two-qubit gate count; results are reported up to 19 evaluation qubits and include an illustrative simulation (p = 0.2) run on IBM's QASM simulator (10,000 shots) to show measurement/estimation behavior at a small scale.
experimental_setup: Circuits implementing QAE for a single-step T-Bill expectation were constructed and transpiled for multiple backends/topologies. Backends considered: an ideal all-to-all IBM model, IBM Yorktown (5 qubits, bow-tie), IBM Tokyo (20 qubits, heavy-hex subset), IBM Cairo (27 qubits, Falcon r5.11 family), and an IonQ ion-trap model (all-to-all, MS/RXX native two-qubit interaction). Transpilation and native-gate decomposition done via Qiskit; two-qubit gate counts were extracted post-transpile. Simulations were performed up to 19 evaluation qubits. An example probabilistic measurement simulation (p=0.2) was run on IBM QASM simulator with 10,000 shots.
dataset_used: Synthetic single-step T-Bill binomial model: two outcomes (V_low -> |0>, V_high -> |1>) with probability p for the high outcome. Example p=0.2 used for illustrative measurement simulation. No external financial dataset was used.

steps: Define simplified financial model and map outcomes to a single objective qubit state prepared by A = RY(θ).
Construct QAE circuit: prepare n evaluation qubits with Hadamards, implement controlled-Q/CRY gates from evaluation qubits to the objective qubit, and add inverse QFT on evaluation qubits.
Optimize circuit layout to reduce SWAPs where possible (manual order changes and transpiler optimizations).
Transpile/decompose circuits per backend (IBM and IonQ native gates) using Qiskit, producing backend-native gate sequences and performing routing (SWAP insertion) as required by topology.

Count post-transpilation two-qubit gates (CX or RXX/MS equivalents) for each circuit and backend. For IBM real-device topologies (Tokyo, Cairo) repeat for multiple initial qubit placements/transpile runs to capture routing variability.
Aggregate counts across runs and fit polynomial models (second-order) to gate-count vs. n data to extract leading-order scaling coefficients and compare device families.

key_findings: [supported] Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) can be used to estimate expectation values (e.g., bond/T-Bill pricing) and was applied as the core algorithmic approach in this study.
[supported] QAE provides a theoretical quadratic convergence in estimation error O(M^-1) compared to classical Monte Carlo O(M^-1/2) (equation and citation provided).
[supported] Increasing the number of evaluation qubits increases the accuracy of the QAE estimate but also increases circuit width and depth (more entangling/two-qubit gates required).
[supported] Two-qubit gates dominate circuit complexity and are more challenging (longer execution, higher error) than single-qubit gates.

[supported] On superconducting devices (IBM backends) CRY decompositions typically require two CX gates on that hardware; on ion-trap hardware (IonQ) CRY can be realized using a single MS / RXX entangling gate, reducing two-qubit gate count for that primitive.
[supported] The need for SWAP insertions on fixed-topology superconducting devices increases the total number of two-qubit gates; SWAP is implemented as three CX gates on IBM-style devices.
[supported] The authors measured two-qubit gate counts for QAE circuits (1–19 evaluation qubits) via Qiskit transpilation and found systematic differences between device types and topologies.

[supported] For QAE circuits the analytical (ideal) superconducting all-to-all case yields n^2 + n two-qubit gates, while the ion-trap case (using native MS/RXX) yields n^2 two-qubit gates (n = number of evaluation qubits).

[supported] Empirical polynomial fits from the authors' transpile-based experiments: IonQ ~ n^2 (leading coefficient ≈1), IBM ideal ~ n^2 + n (analytical), IBM Tokyo fit 2.1 n^2 − 4.7 n + 6.8, IBM Cairo fit 3.5 n^2 − 12.8 n + 22.3 (R^2 = 0.9988 reported).

[supported] Across the explored range (1–19 evaluation qubits) the ion-trap (IonQ) circuits required roughly a factor of two to three fewer two-qubit gates than the superconducting-device circuits (as observed in the authors' experiments/transpilation).

[supported] The exact number of SWAPs required on superconducting hardware depends strongly on qubit placement and routing; minimizing SWAPs (qubit routing) is an NP-hard combinatorial problem and mapping heuristics (e.g., SABRE) are stochastic and do not guarantee global optimality.

[speculative] The authors suggest that the observed 2–3× reduction in two-qubit gates for ion-trap systems will translate into materially more efficient/less error-prone financial QAE executions in practice (this extrapolates gate counts to error/performance outcomes beyond the measured gate counts).
results_summary: The paper analyzes how quantum circuit complexity for Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) applied to a simple T-Bill expectation-value problem scales with the number of evaluation qubits on different hardware models. Using Qiskit transpilation and device-specific gate decompositions, the authors count two-qubit gates for ion-trap (IonQ), IBM hypothetical all-to-all, and real IBM superconducting topologies (Tokyo, Cairo) up to 19 evaluation qubits. They find that native ion-trap gates (MS/RXX) and all-to-all connectivity reduce the number of two-qubit gates compared to fixed-topology superconducting devices; empirical polynomial fits indicate leading-order coefficients that imply a roughly 2–3× reduction in two-qubit gate counts for IonQ versus some IBM devices, with routing-induced SWAPs on superconducting hardware being the main source of overhead.
performance_claims: IonQ (ion-trap) observed leading-order scaling ≈ 1·n^2 two-qubit gates for n evaluation qubits (empirical/simulation result).
IBM ideal (all-to-all superconducting hypothetical) analytical scaling = n^2 + n two-qubit gates.
IBM Tokyo empirical polynomial fit: 2.1 n^2 − 4.7 n + 6.8 (R^2 = 0.9988).
IBM Cairo empirical polynomial fit: 3.5 n^2 − 12.8 n + 22.3 (R^2 = 0.9988).

Example small-circuit counts: for 3 evaluation qubits the IBM decomposition required 12 two-qubit gates (after native decomposition) while IonQ required 9 two-qubit gates; IBM Yorktown case with SWAP needed 15 two-qubit gates in that placement example.
Authors report that across experiments from 1 to 19 evaluation qubits, IonQ circuits used ~2–3× fewer two-qubit gates than superconducting-device circuits in their measurements.
QAE estimation error bound provided: |p − p̃| ≤ π/M + π^2/M^2 ≤ O(M^−1) (equation cited).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reiterates the theoretical quadratic advantage of QAE over classical Monte Carlo (error scaling O(M^−1) vs O(M^−1/2)), citing known results, but does not demonstrate a realized quantum computational advantage in practice; their contribution focuses on hardware-dependent circuit cost differences rather than a practical speedup or advantage demonstration.
limitations: The exact number of required SWAP operations is unpredictable because the qubit routing problem is NP-hard (author-stated).

The study is focused only on counting two-qubit gates (CX / MS / RXX) and SWAP-induced overheads, not on other performance metrics such as gate fidelities, noise, decoherence, or end-to-end runtime (author-stated).
Results depend on initial qubit placement and exhibit variability; different placements produce different SWAP counts (author-stated).
The SABRE SWAP mapper is stochastic and cannot guarantee the globally minimal SWAP count (author-stated).
The IBM Yorktown device was omitted for larger-scale experiments because it only has five qubits (author-stated / hardware-availability constraint).
Experiments/simulations were performed up to 19 evaluation qubits (author-stated limit of the empirical study).

The financial model used is a simplified single-period T-Bill (zero-coupon) representation mapped to a single objective qubit; more realistic/multi-period instruments were not implemented (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Ion-trap (all-to-all, MS/RXX native gates) backends require ~2–3x fewer post-transpilation two-qubit gates for QAE circuits than superconducting devices with limited connectivity, indicating a hardware-level advantage for this financial QAE instance.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Limited connectivity in superconducting topologies (IBM Tokyo, Cairo) forces SWAP insertion and substantially increases two-qubit gate counts (empirical fits show large n^2 coefficients), which challenges NISQ feasibility as the number of evaluation qubits grows.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical polynomial fits quantify scaling: IBM Tokyo ~2.1 n^2 - 4.7 n + 6.8 and IBM Cairo ~3.5 n^2 - 12.8 n + 22.3 (R^2≈0.999), while ion-trap models show a smaller leading-order coefficient (~factor 2–3 reduction).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical transpiler routing, manual layout optimizations and repeated placement attempts materially affect post-transpile gate counts; classical tooling is therefore essential to practical circuit scalability.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Study focuses on post-transpilation two-qubit gate counts as proxy for execution difficulty but does not execute on noisy hardware or model noise, leaving actual run-time fidelity and error impacts unquantified.
